title: The Code: four themes and person-centred decisions
blurb: Know the Code's four themes and 25 standards, and use them to make person-centred decisions, including conscientious objection.
question: A nurse on a gynaecology ward has a religious objection to abortion. She is allocated to a woman admitted for a planned termination. Under the NMC Code, what must she do?

teach.body: The Code sets the professional standards of practice and behaviour that every nurse, midwife and nursing associate must uphold. It has 25 numbered standards grouped under four themes: prioritise people, practise effectively, preserve safety, and promote professionalism and trust. The NMC describes its values as not negotiable or discretionary. You commit to them when you join the register and every time you renew, and the NMC can act if you fail to uphold them.

teach.h: The four themes at a glance
head: Theme
Standards
Core idea
rows: Dignity, preferences, needs, best interests, confidentiality
Evidence, communication, teamwork, records, delegation, indemnity
Competence, candour, emergencies, concerns, medicines, harm
teach.caption: Learn the order: People, Practice, Safety, Professionalism (P-P-S-P).

items.label: the only UK nation where nursing associates are regulated

teach.caption: The Code applies to nurses and midwives across the UK and to nursing associates in England.

teach.body: Base every decision on the person's needs and preferences, not on assumptions or on what is convenient for staff. Treat people as individuals and avoid assumptions (1.3); work in partnership and encourage shared decisions (2.1, 2.3); respect the level of involvement each person wants (2.4); respect, support and document their right to accept or refuse care (2.5); and balance acting in their best interests with that right to refuse (4.1).

children.label: Tell colleagues, manager and the person

teach.caption: Statutory rights: Abortion Act 1967 s4 (Great Britain); Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990 s38 (UK-wide).

items: Check the objection is within the limited legal grounds.
Tell your colleagues, your manager and the person receiving care.
Arrange for a suitably qualified colleague to take over that person's care.
Do not express your personal beliefs to the person in an inappropriate way (Code 20.7).
In an emergency to save life or prevent grave permanent injury, take part.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Nurse Amara on the gynaecology ward
teach.body: Amara is allocated to Ms Clarke, 29, admitted for a planned termination. Amara has a religious objection. Abortion is one of the two areas where a legal right to object exists, so she tells the nurse in charge, her manager and Ms Clarke that a colleague will look after her, and makes sure a suitably qualified colleague takes over. She does not share her beliefs with Ms Clarke. If Ms Clarke haemorrhaged and treatment was needed to save her life, Amara would have to help.
teach.cite: NMC Code 4.4, 20.7; NMC conscientious objection page (2023)

teach.h: Evidence and leadership run through all four themes

rows.label: Advice is evidence-based
values: Information and advice must rest on evidence

rows.label: Stay competent
values: Maintain knowledge and skills for safe practice

rows.label: Know your limits
values: Ask for help beyond your competence

teach.caption: Working within competence is described in the Code as a key underpinning principle that should be upheld at all times.

teach.text: Conscientious objection is NOT a general right to opt out of care you disagree with. It is limited to taking part in abortion and in fertility (HFE) treatment, and it falls away when treatment is needed to save life or prevent grave permanent injury.

items: Four themes: prioritise people (1–5), practise effectively (6–12), preserve safety (13–19), promote professionalism and trust (20–25).
Decisions rest on the person's needs and preferences; respect and document the right to refuse (2.5).
Conscientious objection: tell colleagues, manager and the person, and hand over to a suitably qualified colleague (4.4).
Ambassador for the profession: uphold the Code's values inside and outside work (20.1).

summary: You can now name the four themes of the Code with their standard numbers and apply them to person-centred decisions. You can also explain when a conscientious objection is lawful and the steps the Code requires.

A.q: A newly registered nurse is revising the NMC Code. Under which theme does the standard on keeping clear and accurate records sit?
options: Prioritise people
Practise effectively
Preserve safety
Promote professionalism and trust
A.why: Records are standard 10, which sits in 'Practise effectively' (standards 6–12) alongside evidence, communication, teamwork and delegation.

whyNot.0: Prioritise people covers standards 1–5: dignity, preferences, needs, best interests and confidentiality.
whyNot.2: Preserve safety covers 13–19: competence, candour, emergencies, concerns, medicines and reducing harm.
whyNot.3: Promote professionalism and trust covers 20–25: reputation, registration, complaints and leadership.

A.q: Mrs Hughes, 74, has capacity and declines her evening wash, saying she prefers to bathe in the morning. What should the nurse do?
options: Wash her now and explain it is ward routine
Ask her son to encourage her to wash tonight
Report the refusal to the safeguarding lead
Respect her preference and record the plan
A.why: Code 2.5 requires nurses to respect, support and document a person's right to accept or refuse care. Her preference is reasonable and should shape the plan (Code 1.3, 2.1).

whyNot.0: Ward routine is not a reason to override the choice of a person with capacity; that breaches Code 2.5.
whyNot.1: Using a relative to pressure her undermines her own decision about her care.
whyNot.2: Choosing a morning bath is not a safeguarding concern; there is no abuse or neglect here.

A.q: Which group does the NMC Code apply to?
options: Nurses and midwives in the UK and nursing associates in England
Registered nurses in the UK and healthcare assistants in England
Nurses, midwives and nursing associates in all four UK nations
Nurses and nursing associates in the UK and midwives in England
A.why: The Code applies to registered nurses and midwives across the UK and to nursing associates, who are regulated by the NMC in England.

whyNot.1: Healthcare assistants are not on the NMC register, so the Code does not regulate them.
whyNot.2: Nursing associates are regulated in England, not in all four nations.
whyNot.3: Midwives are regulated across the UK, not in England alone.

B.q: A theatre nurse objects to taking part in a planned termination of pregnancy on religious grounds. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Explain her beliefs to the woman so she understands the refusal
Swap shifts informally without telling the manager or the woman
Inform colleagues, manager and the woman, and hand over care
Take part this time and raise her objection at her next appraisal
B.why: Code 4.4: tell colleagues, your manager and the person receiving care about a conscientious objection, and arrange for a suitably qualified colleague to take over that person's care. Abortion is a lawful ground (Abortion Act 1967 s4).

whyNot.0: Code 20.7 says do not express personal beliefs to people in an inappropriate way.
whyNot.1: An informal swap without telling her manager and the woman does not meet Code 4.4.
whyNot.3: She has a lawful right to object to a planned termination and does not need to take part.

B.q: During a planned termination the woman haemorrhages and needs urgent treatment to save her life. A nurse with a conscientious objection is the nearest registrant. What applies?
options: She may decline because her objection was declared in advance
She may assist with observations but not with the treatment
She should wait for a colleague with no objection to arrive
She must help, as the right to object does not cover saving life
B.why: Under Abortion Act 1967 s4, the right to object does not apply where treatment is necessary to save the life, or prevent grave permanent injury, of the pregnant woman.

whyNot.0: Declaring an objection in advance does not extend it to life-saving treatment.
whyNot.1: There is no partial exemption in an emergency; the life-saving exception applies to the treatment itself.
whyNot.2: Waiting would put the woman's life at risk; Code 15 also requires help in an emergency.

B.q: A ward manager suggests that a patient with a learning disability 'won't want' to be involved in discharge planning. Which Code principle best guides the nurse's response?
options: Avoid assumptions and recognise individual choice
Make sure care is delivered without undue delay
Share information when safety outweighs confidentiality
Keep to the laws of the country where you practise
B.why: Code 1.3 requires nurses to avoid making assumptions and to recognise diversity and individual choice; Code 2.3 adds encouraging people to share decisions.

whyNot.1: Code 1.4 is about timeliness, not about involving the person in decisions.
whyNot.2: Code 5.4 concerns sharing information, which is not the issue here.
whyNot.3: Code 20.4 is about obeying the law, which does not address the assumption being made.

C.q: Mr Patel, 81, has capacity. He refuses his prescribed blood-thinning injection after a full explanation of the risk of clots. His daughter asks the nurse to give it while he sleeps. What is the best response?
options: Give it while he sleeps, as it is in his best interests
Ask the doctor to assess his capacity before accepting the refusal
Respect his refusal, document it and inform the prescriber
Agree to give it if his daughter signs the drug chart
C.why: A person with capacity can refuse treatment. Code 4.1 balances best interests with the right to refuse, and Code 2.5 requires the nurse to respect and document the refusal. Informing the prescriber allows a review (Code 13.2).

whyNot.0: Giving treatment covertly to a person with capacity who has refused it is unlawful and breaches Code 4.2.
whyNot.1: Capacity is presumed; an unwise-seeming refusal after a full explanation is not a reason to doubt it.
whyNot.3: A relative cannot consent for an adult with capacity, so her signature changes nothing.

C.q: A nurse posts a comment online mocking a political party while identifying herself as a nurse at a named hospital. Which Code standard is most directly engaged?
options: Standard 5: respect privacy and confidentiality
Standard 13: work within the limits of competence
Standard 20: uphold the reputation of the profession
Standard 24: respond to complaints made against you
C.why: Standard 20 includes not expressing personal beliefs, including political beliefs, inappropriately (20.7) and using social media responsibly (20.10).

whyNot.0: No patient information has been shared, so confidentiality is not the main issue.
whyNot.1: Competence concerns clinical practice, not online conduct.
whyNot.3: No complaint has been made against her.

C.q: A healthcare assistant asks a staff nurse whether nurses who are not in charge are expected to show leadership. What does the Code say?
options: Leadership is expected from ward managers and matrons
Leadership applies after a preceptorship period ends
Leadership duties apply to band 7 nurses and above
All registrants have opportunities to show leadership
C.why: Standard 25 states that all registrants will have opportunities to demonstrate leadership qualities whether or not they occupy formal leadership positions.

whyNot.0: The Code does not limit leadership to managers and matrons.
whyNot.1: There is no preceptorship threshold for leadership in the Code.
whyNot.2: The Code does not link leadership to pay bands.

reteach.title: Think of the Code as four promises
reteach.question: If you remember four promises to the public, can you place any standard?

blocks.body: Promise 1: you put people first (1–5). Promise 2: you do the job well, using evidence, communicating, recording and delegating safely (6–12). Promise 3: you keep people safe, knowing your limits and speaking up (13–19). Promise 4: you behave in a way that earns trust (20–25). Ask which promise a situation tests and you have the theme.

blocks.text: Candour (14) and raising concerns (16) are in PRESERVE SAFETY, not in professionalism. Boundaries and gifts (20, 21) are in PROMOTE PROFESSIONALISM AND TRUST.

explain.body: Treat people as individuals, listen to their preferences, meet their physical, social and psychological needs, act in their best interests and protect their privacy and confidentiality.

test.q: Which standard requires nurses to respect that a person's right to confidentiality continues after death?
options: Standard 5
Standard 7
Standard 10
Standard 17
test.why: Code 5.3: respect that a person's right to privacy and confidentiality continues after they have died.

whyNot.3: Standard 17 is about protecting people who are vulnerable.

explain.body: Use the best available evidence, communicate clearly, work cooperatively, share skills, keep clear records, delegate accountably and hold an indemnity arrangement.

test.q: A nurse delegates a task to a healthcare assistant. Which standard sets out her accountability for that decision?
options: Standard 8
Standard 9
Standard 10
Standard 11
test.why: Standard 11: be accountable for your decisions to delegate tasks and duties to other people.

whyNot.0: Standard 8 is about working cooperatively with colleagues.
whyNot.1: Standard 9 is about sharing skills, knowledge and feedback.
whyNot.2: Standard 10 is about keeping clear and accurate records.

explain.body: Work within your competence, be candid when things go wrong, help in emergencies, act on risks and raise concerns, protect vulnerable people, handle medicines safely and reduce harm, including infection.

test.q: Under which theme does the professional duty of candour appear?
options: Prioritise people
Practise effectively
Preserve safety
Promote professionalism and trust

whyNot.3: Promote professionalism and trust is standards 20–25.

explain.body: Uphold the profession's reputation, keep boundaries, refuse all but trivial gifts, meet registration requirements, cooperate with investigations, respond to complaints and provide leadership.

test.q: Which standard covers telling the NMC and employers about a caution or a criminal charge?
options: Standard 22
Standard 23
Standard 24
Standard 25
test.why: Code 23.2: tell both the NMC and any employers as soon as you can about any caution or charge.

whyNot.0: Standard 22 covers practice hours and CPD for registration.
